description: Nāda arises when the self, wishing to speak, moves the mind, the mind strikes the body's fire and the fire drives the wind up from the knot of Brahmā through navel, heart, throat and head to the mouth, taking five forms from very subtle to artificial.

When the jīva dwells on the petals of the body's centres, particular states arise — e.g. in the moon centre compassion, forbearance, uprightness, fortitude, dispassion, steadiness, joy, laughter, horripilation, tears of meditation, stability, depth, effort, clarity, generosity, one-pointedness.
Success or failure in song depends on the petal on which the jīva rests; dwelling in the brahmarandhra, bathed in nectar, the singer accomplishes music excellently.
Aesthetic rapture: a relish in which consciousness, freed from personal limits and other objects, rests in itself as bliss and wonder — 'the twin of tasting Brahman'.
The state of śānta: neither pain nor pleasure, neither hatred nor envy, equal toward all beings; the natural state from which all emotions arise and into which they return.
The eight involuntary bodily signs of strong feeling: paralysis, sweat, horripilation, change of voice, trembling, change of colour, tears and fainting.
In devotional singing the devotee's voice falters, the heart melts, he weeps again and again, sometimes laughs, and unabashed sings aloud and dances — such a devotee purifies the world.
The sentence's meaning flashes as a single intuition that cannot be described even by the one who has it.
For those in whom light has dawned and whose minds are undisturbed, knowledge of past and future is like perception.
Fiery mantras awaken when the breath flows in the right channel, lunar ones in the left; when the breath flows in both, all mantras awaken and bear fruit.
